title: "Martinec et al. (2018) benchmark specification"

> Martinec, Z., Klemann, V., van der Wal, W., Riva, R. E. M., Spada, G., Sun,
> Y., Melini, D., Kachuck, S. B., Barletta, V., Simon, K., A, G. and James,
> T. S. (2018). A benchmark study of numerical implementations of the sea
> level equation in GIA modelling. *Geophysical Journal International* 215(1),
> 389-414. doi:[10.1093/gji/ggy280](https://doi.org/10.1093/gji/ggy280)

This page tells a solver developer what to run for benchmark cases A to E and
what to compare the result against. The facts come from the paper. The text,
the order and the tables are our own. Page numbers refer to the journal
pagination, and equation, table and figure numbers refer to the paper.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this page is not the authority

The repository records the case facts in files that a program can read. Where
this page and those files disagree, report it, and use the files until the
disagreement is settled.

- The five cases: `giamip/resources/cases/benchmarks/martinec2018/A.json` to `E.json`, shown in
  [the Martinec (2018) collection page](../collections/martinec2018.qmd).
- The earth model: `giamip/resources/models/m3-l70-v01.json`, shown in
  [the earth models](../reference/earth-models.qmd).
- The ice heights, time scenarios and ocean basins: `giamip/resources/loads/martinec2018.json`,
  shown in [the loads and grids](../reference/loads-and-grids.qmd).
- The signs and datums of each quantity:
  [the conventions](../reference/conventions.qmd).
- The known defects in the benchmark data:
  [the corrections](../data/corrections.qmd).
:::

## Notation

Positions on the sphere are $\Omega = (\theta, \lambda)$, with colatitude
$\theta$ and longitude $\lambda$ in degrees. Time $t$ starts at $t_0 = 0$,
when the load is first applied, and ends at the terminal time $t_f$. The
symbols follow [the conventions](../reference/conventions.qmd): $U$ is the
vertical displacement of the solid surface, $N$ the geoid displacement, $S$
the sea-surface variation, $\zeta$ the solid Earth topography and $h_{UF}$ the
thickness of the uniform water layer. The relative sea level (RSL in the
conventions table) is written $s$ in the equations. The ocean function
$\mathcal{O}(\Omega, t)$ is 1 over the ocean and 0 over land. The ice density
is $\rho_{ice}$ and the water density is $\rho_w$. $\Omega_0$ is the full
solid angle, $4\pi$.

## Physical assumptions

All five cases share these assumptions (p. 390):

- The reference frame is the centre of mass frame.
- The earth model is incompressible and does not rotate. There is no
  rotational feedback.
- There is no ocean circulation, so the sea surface stays an equipotential
  surface at all times.
- Water moves between ice and ocean immediately. No water is stored on land or
  in the atmosphere.
- The ice and water densities are constant.
- The Earth is in isostatic equilibrium at $t_0$ (p. 390).

## Earth model

All cases use M3-L70-V01, the model of Spada et al. (2011), table 3 (p. 393,
section 3.1). It is spherically symmetric, self-gravitating and
incompressible, with five layers. The lithosphere is elastic, the three mantle
layers are Maxwell viscoelastic, and the core is a uniform inviscid fluid. The
paper does not repeat the layer values. The table below is generated from
`giamip/resources/models/m3-l70-v01.json`.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path("../..").resolve()))
from IPython.display import Markdown
from giamip import cases

# The earth model is read from the JSON file so that this page and the model
# file cannot disagree. The paper only names the model (section 3.1).
model = cases.earth_model("m3-l70-v01")
rows = ["| Layer | Top radius (km) | Bottom radius (km) | Density (kg/m3) | Shear modulus (Pa) | Viscosity (Pa s) | Rheology |",
        "| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |"]
for layer in model["layers"]:
    # A null viscosity marks the elastic lithosphere, which has no viscous flow.
    eta = layer["viscosity_pa_s"]
    eta_text = "none (elastic)" if eta is None else f"{eta:.1e}"
    rows.append(f"| {layer['role']} | {layer['top_radius_km']} | "
                f"{layer['bottom_radius_km']} | {layer['density_kg_m3']} | "
                f"{layer['shear_modulus_pa']:.4e} | {eta_text} | {layer['rheology']} |")
rows.append("")
rows.append(f"Compressible: {model['compressible']}. "
            f"Self-gravitating: {model['self_gravitating']}.")
Markdown("\n".join(rows))
```

## Load

### Densities

The ice load is a surface mass density (p. 393, eq. 28):

$$
\sigma_{ice}(\Omega, t) = \rho_{ice}\, h_{ice}(\Omega, t)
$$ {#eq-m18-ice-load}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 28.) The total surface load is the ice plus the
water that the sea level equation puts on the ocean, both relative to $t_0$:

$$
\sigma(\Omega, t) = \sigma_{ice}(\Omega, t) + \rho_w\, s(\Omega, t)
$$ {#eq-m18-total-load}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 2.)

The benchmark densities are $\rho_{ice} = 931$ kg/m3 and $\rho_w = 1000$
kg/m3 (p. 390). They differ from the GIAMIP values. A solver must read the
densities from the case, never from a shared constant.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Both columns come from the repository files, so a change to either file
# shows here. The benchmark values are also stated on p. 390 of the paper.
m18 = cases.loads("martinec2018")["constants"]
giamip = cases.case("giamip-exp01")["constants"]
Markdown(f"""
| Quantity | Martinec (2018) | GIAMIP |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ice density (kg/m3) | {m18['ice_density_kg_m3']} | {giamip['ice_density_kg_m3']} |
| Ocean water density (kg/m3) | {m18['water_density_kg_m3']} | {giamip['ocean_water_density_kg_m3']} |
""")
```

### Spherical cap

Every case uses one spherical cap shape, the cap of Spada et al. (2011),
table 4, row 1, with maximum height $h_0$ and angular radius $\alpha_0 =
10^\circ$ (p. 393). The paper does not write the height profile of the cap. It
states that the cap has an infinite slope at its edge, and that this slope
causes spikes in the differences at the cap edge (p. 399). Three placements
and heights are defined.

Ice height models. Source: Martinec et al. (2018), table 1.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Table 1 of the paper, read from giamip/resources/loads/martinec2018.json.
loads = cases.loads("martinec2018")
rows = ["| Model | Centre colatitude $\\theta_0$ | Centre longitude $\\lambda_0$ | $h_0$ (m) | Angular radius $\\alpha_0$ |",
        "| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |"]
for name in ["L0", "L1", "L2"]:
    m = loads["ice_height_models"][name]
    rows.append(f"| {name} | {m['centre_colatitude_deg']}° | {m['centre_longitude_deg']}° | "
                f"{m['height_m']} | {loads['load_shape']['angular_radius_deg']}° |")
Markdown("\n".join(rows))
```

L1 is thick, so it never floats. L2 is 500 m high, so it satisfies the
floating condition (@eq-m18-hw-star) when it reaches the coast of basin B2
(p. 394).

### Time scenarios

Both the height $h(t)$ and the angular radius $\alpha(t)$ of the cap change
with time. Source: Martinec et al. (2018), table 2.

| Scenario | $t_0$ to $t_1$ | $t_1$ to $t_2$ | Terminal time $t_f$ |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| T0 | Step load at $t_0$: $h = h_0$ and $\alpha = \alpha_0$ for $t \in (t_0, t_1]$, $t_1 = 10$ kyr | not used | $t_1 = 10$ kyr |
| T1 | $h$ and $\alpha$ increase linearly from 0 at $t_0$ to $h_0$ and $\alpha_0$ at $t_1 = 10$ kyr | $h = h_0$ and $\alpha = \alpha_0$ for $t \in (t_1, t_2]$ | $t_2 = 15$ kyr |

For case C, the paper reports that the grounded ice mass grows approximately
as the cube of time up to 10 kyr and is constant after that (p. 403, Fig. 8).

## Initial topography and ocean basins

The solid Earth topography at $t_0$ is an exponential basin with its centre at
$(\theta_b, \lambda_b)$ (p. 395):

$$
\zeta^{(0)}(\Omega) = b_{max} - b_0 \exp\!\left(-\frac{\psi^2}{2\sigma_b^2}\right)
$$ {#eq-m18-basin}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 29.) Here $\psi$ is the angular distance from the
basin centre,

$$
\cos\psi = \cos\theta \cos\theta_b + \sin\theta \sin\theta_b \cos(\lambda - \lambda_b)
$$ {#eq-m18-psi}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 30), and $\sigma_b = 26^\circ$ in all cases. The
minimum of $\zeta^{(0)}$ is $b_{max} - b_0$ at the basin centre and the maximum
is $b_{max}$ at the antipode. The initial ocean function follows from the
topography:

$$
\mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \zeta^{(0)}(\Omega) < 0, \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-m18-ocean-initial}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 1.) The basin radius, where $\zeta^{(0)} = 0$, is
$\psi_0 = 24.85^\circ$ for both B1 and B2 (p. 395). This value equals
$\sigma_b \sqrt{2 \ln(b_0 / b_{max})}$. For B2 the paper gives the radius as
$24.8503^\circ$ and the initial ocean area as $(1 - \cos\psi_0)/2 = 0.0462956$
of the full sphere (p. 409, Fig. 17).

Ocean basin parameters at $t_0$. Source: Martinec et al. (2018), table 3.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Table 3 of the paper, read from giamip/resources/loads/martinec2018.json. The minimum
# topography b_max - b_0 is computed here and is the (negative) ocean depth
# at the basin centre.
basins = loads["ocean_basins"]
rows = ["| Model | $\\theta_b$ | $\\lambda_b$ | $b_{max}$ (m) | $b_0$ (m) | $\\sigma_b$ | $b_{max} - b_0$ (m) |",
        "| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |"]
for name in ["B0", "B1", "B2"]:
    b = basins[name]
    rows.append(f"| {name} | {b['centre_colatitude_deg']}° | {b['centre_longitude_deg']}° | "
                f"{b['bmax_m']} | {b['b0_m']} | {basins['sigma_b_deg']}° | {b['bmax_m'] - b['b0_m']} |")
Markdown("\n".join(rows))
```

B0 has no ocean. B1 lies far from the ice. B2 is deep and lies next to the ice
cap, so a growing L2 cap reaches its coast. B2\* has the B2 parameters, but
@eq-m18-basin then gives the topography at $t_f$ (case E).

## Sea level equation

### Definitions

The sea level height $h_w$ is the water column from the ocean bottom to the
sea surface. The relative sea level is its change since $t_0$:

$$
s(\Omega, t) = h_w(\Omega, t) - h_w(\Omega, t_0)
$$ {#eq-m18-rsl-def}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 3.) The paper defines $S(\Omega, t)$ "as the radial
distance of the sea surface at time $t$ relative to the radial distance of the
sea surface at time $t_0$" (p. 391):

$$
S(\Omega, t) = r_w(\Omega, t) - r_w(\Omega, t_0)
$$ {#eq-m18-sea-surface}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 4), with $r_w$ the distance from the geocentre to
the sea surface. With $U$ the vertical displacement of the ocean bottom,

$$
s(\Omega, t) = S(\Omega, t) - U(\Omega, t)
$$ {#eq-m18-rsl}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 5.) The geoid displacement is

$$
N(\Omega, t) = -\frac{\Phi(\Omega, t)}{g_0}
$$ {#eq-m18-geoid}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 9), where $\Phi$ is the increment of the
gravitational potential and $g_0$ is the unperturbed gravity at the surface.

The sea level equation splits $s$ into a uniform layer over the ocean and a
part that varies in space:

$$
s(\Omega, t) = h_{UF}(t)\, \mathcal{O}(\Omega, t) + s_{NU}(\Omega, t)
$$ {#eq-m18-sle}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 6.) $s_{NU}$ follows from the condition that the
sea surface is an equipotential surface. $h_{UF}$ follows from conservation
of mass in the ice and ocean system:

$$
\int_{\Omega_0} \sigma(\Omega, t)\, d\Omega = 0
$$ {#eq-m18-mass}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 10.)

### Variants

The cases use three levels of the sea level equation (p. 395, section 3.4).

| SLE | Ocean function | Ice over the ocean | Equations | Cases |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | No ocean | Not applicable | Load is $\sigma_{ice}$ only | A |
| 1 | Fixed at $\mathcal{O}^{(0)}$ | Removed at the coast | @eq-m18-fixed-ice, @eq-m18-fixed-snu, @eq-m18-fixed-huf | B, C |
| 2 | Changes with time, with grounded and floating ice | Grounded or floating | @eq-m18-hw, @eq-m18-hw-star, @eq-m18-ocean-float, @eq-m18-float-snu, @eq-m18-moving-huf | D, E |

### SLE = 1: fixed ocean geometry

The ocean function is $\mathcal{O}(\Omega, t) = \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)$ at
all times. Ice is not allowed on the ocean. Any ice over the ocean function is
deleted before the load is applied:

$$
\sigma_{ice}(\Omega, t) = \sigma_{ice}(\Omega, t) \left[1 - \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)\right]
$$ {#eq-m18-fixed-ice}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 7.) This is how case C removes ("calves") the part
of the cap that reaches the coast. The non-uniform part is

$$
s_{NU}(\Omega, t) = \left[N(\Omega, t) - U(\Omega, t)\right] \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)
$$ {#eq-m18-fixed-snu}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 8.) Mass conservation gives the uniform layer:

$$
h_{UF}(t) = -\frac{1}{\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{(0)}} \left[\frac{1}{\rho_w}\, \bar{\sigma}_{ice}(t) + \overline{NU}(t)\right]
$$ {#eq-m18-fixed-huf}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 12), with the integrals

$$
\bar{\sigma}_{ice}(t) = \int_{\Omega_0} \sigma_{ice}(\Omega, t)\left[1 - \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)\right] d\Omega,
\qquad
\overline{NU}(t) = \int_{\Omega_0} \left[N(\Omega, t) - U(\Omega, t)\right] \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)\, d\Omega
$$ {#eq-m18-fixed-integrals}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 13) and the ocean area

$$
\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{(0)} = \int_{\Omega_0} \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)\, d\Omega
$$ {#eq-m18-fixed-area}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 14.) In @eq-m18-fixed-huf the first term is the
water taken from the ocean to build the ice, and the second term is the water
that the change of $N - U$ over the ocean needs. The paper plots the two terms
separately for case C (p. 405, Fig. 11).

### SLE = 2: moving coastline and floating ice

The water column at time $t$ is computed from the initial topography:

$$
h_w(\Omega, t) = h_{UF}(t) + N(\Omega, t) - U(\Omega, t) - \zeta^{(0)}(\Omega)
$$ {#eq-m18-hw}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 15.) The water column left after the ice has
displaced water is

$$
h_w^*(\Omega, t) = h_w(\Omega, t) - \frac{1}{\rho_w}\, \sigma_{ice}(\Omega, t)
$$ {#eq-m18-hw-star}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 22.) The ice is grounded where $h_w^* \le 0$ and
floats where $h_w^* > 0$. The ocean function is

$$
\mathcal{O}(\Omega, t) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } h_w(\Omega, t) > 0 \text{ and } h_w^*(\Omega, t) > 0, \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-m18-ocean-float}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 23.) The non-uniform part is

$$
s_{NU}(\Omega, t) = \left[N(\Omega, t) - U(\Omega, t) - \frac{1}{\rho_w}\, \sigma_{ice}(\Omega, t)\right] \mathcal{O}(\Omega, t) - \zeta^{(0)}(\Omega)\left[\mathcal{O}(\Omega, t) - \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)\right]
$$ {#eq-m18-float-snu}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 24.) Without floating ice, the $\sigma_{ice}$ term
is absent and the expression reduces to eq. 17 of the paper. The second term
acts only where the coastline has moved since $t_0$. Mass conservation gives

$$
h_{UF}(t) = -\frac{1}{\bar{\mathcal{O}}(t)} \left[\frac{1}{\rho_w}\, \bar{\sigma}_{ice}(t) + \overline{NU}(t) - \bar{\zeta}^{(0)}(t)\right]
$$ {#eq-m18-moving-huf}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 19.) Here $\bar{\sigma}_{ice}$ and $\overline{NU}$
are the integrals of @eq-m18-fixed-integrals with $\mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)$
replaced by $\mathcal{O}(\Omega, t)$, and

$$
\bar{\zeta}^{(0)}(t) = \int_{\Omega_0} \zeta^{(0)}(\Omega)\left[\mathcal{O}(\Omega, t) - \mathcal{O}^{(0)}(\Omega)\right] d\Omega
$$ {#eq-m18-moving-zeta}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 20),

$$
\bar{\mathcal{O}}(t) = \int_{\Omega_0} \mathcal{O}(\Omega, t)\, d\Omega
$$ {#eq-m18-moving-area}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 21.) @eq-m18-moving-huf holds with and without
floating ice, because the mass of ice removed at the coast equals the mass of
water that floating ice displaces (p. 393, eqs 26 and 27).

$h_{UF}$, $s_{NU}$ and $\mathcal{O}$ depend on $U$ and $N$, and $U$ and $N$
depend on the load. The solver must therefore find the load, the ocean
geometry and the response together.

### Case E: topography prescribed at the terminal time

In case E, @eq-m18-basin with the B2 parameters is the topography that the
solution must reach at $t_f$:

$$
\zeta^{(t),des}(\Omega) = b_{max} - b_0 \exp\!\left(-\frac{\psi^2}{2\sigma_b^2}\right)
$$ {#eq-m18-e-target}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 32.) The topography at $t_f$ follows from the
initial topography and the solution:

$$
\zeta^{(t)}(\Omega) = \zeta^{(0)}(\Omega) + U(\Omega, t_f) - N(\Omega, t_f) - h_{UF}(t_f)
$$ {#eq-m18-e-terminal}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 33.) The ocean geometry depends on $\zeta^{(0)}$,
so @eq-m18-e-terminal cannot be inverted in one step. The paper updates the
initial topography after each full run $k$:

$$
\zeta^{(0),k+1} = \zeta^{(0),k} + \zeta^{(t),des} - \zeta^{(t),k}
$$ {#eq-m18-e-iteration}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 34.) The iteration stops when the L2 norm of
$\zeta^{(t),des} - \zeta^{(t),k}$ is less than 0.01 m. In the paper this
took at most six iterations (p. 409).

## The five cases

```{python}
#| echo: false
# The option columns and the terminal time come from the case files, which
# transcribe table 4 and table 2 of the paper. The last two columns are what
# the paper compares for each case (section 5 and figures 3 to 19); they are
# written here from the paper because the case files do not record them per
# profile.
compared = {
    "A": ("U, N on the ice profile", "none"),
    "B": ("U, N on the ice profile; U, N, S on the basin profile", "none"),
    "C": ("U, N on the ice profile; U, N, S on the basin profile",
          "grounded ice mass; h_UF(t) (reference solution only)"),
    "D": ("U, N on the ice profile; U, N, S on the basin profile",
          "grounded and floating ice mass; h_UF(t); ocean area"),
    "E": ("none", "ocean area; h_UF(t)"),
}
rows = ["| Case | SLE | Ice height | Time | Basin | $t_f$ (kyr) | Profiles at $t_f$ | Time series |",
        "| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- |"]
for c in cases.cases("martinec2018"):
    s = c["specification"]
    letter = c["published_name"].split()[-1]
    profiles, series = compared[letter]
    rows.append(f"| {letter} | {s['sea_level_equation']} | {s['ice_height_model']} | "
                f"{s['time_scenario']} | {s['ocean_basin']} | {s['terminal_time_kyr']} | "
                f"{profiles} | {series} |")
Markdown("\n".join(rows))
```

Option columns source: Martinec et al. (2018), table 4. Terminal times
source: table 2.

**Case A.** Cap L0 sits on the north pole and is applied as a step (T0). There
is no ocean and the sea level equation is not solved. The run is the cap-load
case of Spada et al. (2011) test 1/2. The degree 0 and degree 1 components of
the load are left out (p. 399). Compare $U$ and $N$ at 10 kyr.

**Case B.** Cap L1 (1500 m) at $(25^\circ, 75^\circ)$ is applied as a step
(T0). Basin B1 at $(100^\circ, 320^\circ)$ is far away, and the ice never
reaches it. Solve the sea level equation with the fixed ocean function
(SLE = 1). The load includes spherical harmonic degrees 0 to 256 (p. 401).
Compare at 10 kyr.

**Case C.** Cap L2 (500 m) at $(25^\circ, 75^\circ)$ grows to full size over
10 kyr and then stays constant to 15 kyr (T1). Basin B2 at $(35^\circ,
25^\circ)$ is close, and the cap reaches its coast. The ocean function stays
fixed (SLE = 1), so ice that crosses the coast is removed by
@eq-m18-fixed-ice. Compare at 15 kyr.

**Case D.** As case C, with SLE = 2. The ocean function is recomputed from
@eq-m18-ocean-float, so the coast moves and ice past the coast can ground or
float. Compare at 15 kyr. The paper reports that $U$ and $N$ are about 10 per
cent larger than in case C, because grounded ice now loads the shelf (p. 405).

**Case E.** As case D, with basin B2\*. The B2 topography is the target at
$t_f = 15$ kyr, and the initial topography is found with
@eq-m18-e-iteration. Compare the ocean area and $h_{UF}(t)$ with case D. The
paper reports a larger ocean area and less water taken from the ocean than in
case D (p. 409).

## Numerical settings

The paper prescribes no common truncation degree, grid, time step or number of
iterations. Each code used its own settings. The reference solution uses the
VEGA settings in the first row. Source: Martinec et al. (2018), table 5 for
the parametrisation and section 4 (pp. 396 to 398) for the settings. A blank
cell means that the paper does not state the value.

| Code (label) | Parametrisation | Spherical harmonic truncation | Spatial grid for load and topography | Time step | Iterations of the sea level equation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VEGA (ZM), reference | time domain, radial finite elements, spherical harmonics | degree 0 to 256; case A from degree 2 | Gauss-Legendre, 1024 latitudes by 2048 longitudes | 20 yr | explicit time differencing, no iteration |
| VILMA (VK) | time domain, radial finite elements, spherical harmonics | 256 for cases A and E, 128 for B, C and D | Gauss-Legendre, 1024 by 2048 | 20 yr | explicit time differencing, no iteration |
| TABOO and SELEN 4 (MS) | Laplace domain, normal modes | | case A analytic; B to E equal-area icosahedral grid, 75 692 pixels of radius 46.3 km | 0.5 kyr | 5 |
| TUDSLE (WW) | Laplace domain, pseudo-spectral | | equal-angle, 0.03125° for A, 0.25° for B | 1 kyr | until the mean relative change is below a threshold, at most 6 per time step |
| MUSSEL (YS) | Laplace domain, pseudo-spectral | 256 | Gaussian, 1024 by 2048 | 100 yr | |
| PGCcalc (KS) | Laplace domain, pseudo-spectral | 256 | equal-angle, 0.125°, fixed shorelines | | |
| TSec02 (VB) | Laplace domain, pseudo-spectral with TABOO Love numbers | | | | |
| A13 (GA) | Laplace domain, semi-analytic | | | | until converged, usually fewer than 3 |
| AFCAL (WWa), case A only | time domain, axisymmetric finite elements, spherical harmonics for the potential | 120 | elements of 0.25°, Poisson ratio 0.495 | | 4 |
| giapy (SK) | time domain with TABOO Love numbers | | equal-angle, 721 latitudes by 512 longitudes | 20 yr | until one more iteration changes the surface by less than 1 per cent on average |

Radial discretisation, where stated: VEGA uses 165 linear elements with steps
of 5, 10 and 40 km in the lithosphere, upper mantle and lower mantle. VILMA
uses 248 elements with steps of 2.5 km in the lithosphere and upper mantle,
10 km in the transition zone and 40 km in the lower mantle (p. 396). VILMA
cannot run with a fixed coastline, so for cases B and C it replaces the
bathymetry with a step of 500 m water depth or 500 m land height (p. 396).

The VEGA convergence test uses case D with four resolutions. Source: Martinec
et al. (2018), table A1.

| Run | Truncation degree $j_{max}$ | Gauss-Legendre grid for the sea level equation |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| C1 | 64 | 256 by 512 |
| C2 | 128 | 256 by 512 |
| C3 | 128 | 512 by 1024 |
| C4 | 256 | 512 by 1024 |

## Outputs

All quantities are in metres and are changes since $t_0$, except the
topography, the ocean area and the ice mass. Upward means away from the
geocentre. See [the conventions](../reference/conventions.qmd) for how the
stored data files depart from these definitions.

| Quantity | Definition | Positive direction | Datum |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $U$ | Vertical displacement of the solid surface (the ocean bottom in the ocean) | Upward | Surface at $t_0$ |
| $N$ | Geoid displacement, $-\Phi/g_0$ (@eq-m18-geoid) | Upward | Geoid at $t_0$ |
| $S$ | Sea-surface variation (@eq-m18-sea-surface) | Upward | Sea surface at $t_0$ |
| $s$ | Relative sea level, $S - U$ (@eq-m18-rsl) | Sea level rising against the bottom | Water column at $t_0$ |
| $h_{UF}$ | Uniform water layer (@eq-m18-fixed-huf, @eq-m18-moving-huf) | Water added to the ocean; negative while ice grows | Zero at $t_0$ |
| $\zeta^{(0)}$ | Solid Earth topography at $t_0$ | Upward; negative in the ocean | Sea surface at $t_0$ |
| $\bar{\mathcal{O}}(t)$ | Ocean area (@eq-m18-moving-area) | Not signed | Plotted as a percentage of $4\pi$ |
| Ice mass | Grounded ice, and floating ice in case D | Not signed | Plotted in units of $10^{17}$ kg |

## Comparison method

**Reference.** The paper has no analytic solution. Each code is compared with
the VEGA solution computed with the settings above (p. 399). The paper calls
it VEGA^ref^.

**Profiles.** All profiles run along a meridian, as a function of colatitude
from 0 to 180 degrees. The differences are measured only over a colatitude
interval.

| Case | Meridian | Passes through | Epoch | Quantities | Difference interval | Figure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | $\lambda = 0^\circ$ | ice centre at the pole | 10 kyr | $U$, $N$ | 0° to 20° | 3 |
| B | $\lambda = 75^\circ$ | ice centre $(25^\circ, 75^\circ)$ | 10 kyr | $U$, $N$ | 5° to 45° | 5 |
| B | $\lambda = 320^\circ$ | basin centre $(100^\circ, 320^\circ)$ | 10 kyr | $U$, $N$, $S$ | 65° to 135° | 6 |
| C | $\lambda = 75^\circ$ | ice centre | 15 kyr | $U$, $N$ | 5° to 45° | 9 |
| C | $\lambda = 25^\circ$ | basin centre $(35^\circ, 25^\circ)$ | 15 kyr | $U$, $N$, $S$ | 0° to 70° | 10 |
| D | $\lambda = 75^\circ$ | ice centre | 15 kyr | $U$, $N$ | 5° to 45° | 14 |
| D | $\lambda = 25^\circ$ | basin centre | 15 kyr | $U$, $N$, $S$ | 0° to 70° | 15 |

**Time series.** Grounded ice mass for case C (Fig. 8); grounded and floating
ice mass for case D (Fig. 13); $h_{UF}(t)$ for cases C, D and E (Figs 11, 16
and 19); ocean area for cases D and E (Figs 17 and 18). All run from 0 to
15 kyr.

**Metrics.** For a quantity $q$ sampled at $n$ points $i$ inside the
difference interval at a fixed time, with $q^{ref}$ the reference value:

$$
\epsilon_q^{RMS} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(q_i - q_i^{ref}\right)^2},
\qquad
\epsilon_q^{MAX} = \max_i \left|q_i - q_i^{ref}\right|
$$ {#eq-m18-metrics}

(Martinec et al. 2018, eq. 31.) The paper plots these metrics for the ice
profiles of cases A to D in Fig. 20 and for the basin profiles of cases B to D
in Fig. 21.

**Features to check.** In case A, the maximum of $U$ (the peripheral bulge) is
14.1° from the ice centre (p. 399). In case B, the same maximum is about
14.1° from the ice centre. The basin edge is at $\theta = 75.7^\circ$, with
bulges at $70.4^\circ$ outside and $80.6^\circ$ inside the basin (p. 402).

## How the reference is built

The reference is VEGA in every case. The converter stores the curves that
scoring compares with in the group `reference` of each converted file, and
each curve carries attributes that say how it was built. The case file's
`reference_data.reference_curves` gives the rule for each profile, and the
table below is generated from those files.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# One row per compared profile and time series, read from the case files.
rows = ["| Case | Curve | Method | Member | Correction |",
        "| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |"]
for letter in "ABCDE":
    curves = cases.case(f"martinec2018-{letter}")["reference_data"]["reference_curves"]
    for profile, rule in curves.get("profiles", {}).items():
        rows.append(f"| {letter} | {profile} profile | {rule['method']} | {rule['member']} | "
                    f"{rule.get('correction', '')} |")
    if "time_series" in curves:
        rule = curves["time_series"]
        rows.append(f"| {letter} | time series | {rule['method']} | {rule['member']} | "
                    f"{rule.get('correction', '')} |")
Markdown("\n".join(rows))
```

**As shipped** copies VEGA's own curve (member ZM) from the archive.
**Recovered** is YS's profile minus YS's own difference file, on YS's grid of
2048 colatitudes from 0.044° to 179.956°. It is used where the shipped VEGA
file is not the curve the published difference files were computed against:

- In case A, the shipped VEGA file is a second run
  (correction `benchmarkA-vega-supplied-run-differs`).
- In the case B basin profile and both case D profiles, the shipped VEGA file
  has 359 rows (correction `martinec2018-caseD-vega-profile-grid`).

**The evidence.** For a contributor, its "recovery" is its profile minus its
own difference file, on the difference file's grid. Every recovery is VEGA as
that contributor's difference file saw it. A cubic spline through the YS
recovery, evaluated on 0° to 180°, reproduces the recovery of every other
contributor at that contributor's own points, colatitude 0° and 180°
included, to these maxima in metres:

| Profile | $U$ | $N$ | $S$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A, ice | 1.7e-4 | 5.9e-5 | |
| B, basin | 3.7e-6 | 6.0e-6 | 8.7e-7 |
| D, ice | 3.2e-6 | 1.3e-5 | |
| D, basin | 8.6e-7 | 2.0e-6 | 2.0e-7 |

The largest values come from VK and WW_axisymmetric in case A, which differ
from the other five codes by 1.6e-4 m at the pole, and from SK in case D. So
every difference file of a case was computed against one VEGA profile, and
the YS recovery gives it. In case A the five recoveries of GA, GS, KS, VB and
WW agree to 6e-14 m and give $U = -302.59759412$ m at the pole, the value of
the one-row VEGA file in the first case A archive. In the case B basin, the
359 shipped rows equal the recoveries of GA, KS and VK to 7e-15 m and of VB to
1e-8 m, so the shipped rows are exact samples of the finer profile. Linear
interpolation between them misses it by up to 0.17 m near the coast. In case
A, both WW variants count as contributors.

**How a result is scored.** `giamip.benchmarks.metrics.score` compares a
profile on the result's own points inside the difference interval, with the
reference evaluated there by the same cubic spline, and a time series on the
result's own times, with the reference interpolated linearly. Scored this way,
every contributor of the archive gets the maximum and RMS of its own
published difference file to 1e-4 m (2e-4 m in case A), which
`tests/test_scoring.py` checks.

## Reported agreement

The numbers below are the largest differences from VEGA^ref^ that the paper
reports. Source: section 5 and section 6 (pp. 399 to 410).

| Case and profile | Solutions | Max $\lvert\Delta U\rvert$ (m) | Max $\lvert\Delta N\rvert$ (m) | RMS $\Delta U$ (m) | RMS $\Delta N$ (m) | Other |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| A, ice | all except SK | 0.7 | 0.03 | 0.2 | 0.01 | about 1.5 per cent of the signal |
| A, ice | AFCAL | 1.7 at the cap edge; 0.3 at the maximum | 0.11 | | | $\Delta N$ oscillates with a wavelength of about 300 km |
| B, basin | eight solutions | 4 | 0.20 | 0.8 | 0.03 | offset in $S$ from $h_{UF}$ up to 0.12 m |
| C, basin | five solutions | | | | | smaller than case B; offset in $S$ of 0.2 m |
| E | SK | | | | | $S$ differs by 0.2 m; $h_{UF}(t)$ differs from ZM, VK and YS |
| All cases | all | 1.5 | 0.1 | 0.5 | 0.02 | about 1.5 per cent; offset in $S$ up to 0.2 m |
| D, ice, VEGA C4 against VEGA^ref^ | VEGA | 0.23 | 0.02 | 0.06 | 0.004 | offset of 1 cm in $S$ from the quadrature for $h_{UF}$ |

For case B on the ice profile, the paper gives no numbers. It reports that
the differences are similar to case A, except for VB, and larger than in case
A for MS, VB and WW (p. 401). For case D, it reports that the differences are
similar to case C (p. 406). For the Laplace-domain codes, the paper reports
time steps between 0.1 and 1 kyr, at most six iterations, and a relative
precision better than 1 per cent (p. 411).

## Values the paper leaves unstated or ambiguous

1. **Cap profile.** The paper does not write the height of the cap as a
   function of distance from its centre. It refers to Spada et al. (2011),
   table 4, row 1.
2. **Cap growth in T1.** Table 2 makes both $h(t)$ and $\alpha(t)$ linear in
   time. The paper does not state how the cap profile scales with $\alpha(t)$,
   or whether the load changes continuously or in steps.
3. **Basin radius formula.** On p. 395 the formula for $\psi_0$ is printed as
   $\sigma_b\sqrt{\ln(b_0/b_{max})^2}$, which gives $11.88^\circ$. The stated
   value $24.85^\circ$, and the $24.8503^\circ$ of Fig. 17, match
   $\sigma_b\sqrt{2\ln(b_0/b_{max})}$.
4. **Degree 0 and 1.** Case A leaves out load degrees 0 and 1, and case B
   includes degrees 0 to 256. The paper does not state the treatment of
   degrees 0 and 1 for cases C, D and E, apart from the centre of mass frame.
5. **Constants.** The paper does not give $g_0$ in @eq-m18-geoid or the Earth
   radius. It does not state the sign convention of $\Phi$.
6. **Case E iteration.** The paper does not state the initial estimate
   $\zeta^{(0),0}$, or the domain and normalisation of the L2 norm in the
   stopping test.
7. **Case E contributors.** Table 6 lists five codes for case E, including MS.
   Figs 18 and 19 show only four: ZM, VK, YS and SK.
8. **Output sampling.** The paper does not state the colatitude spacing of the
   profiles or the time spacing of the time series.
9. **Case E profiles.** The paper shows no profile comparison of $U$, $N$ or
   $S$ for case E.
